articles.title: In National Geographic’s Expedition: Saving Our Seas, it’s all hands on deck
articles.text:
In 'Expedition: Saving Our Seas,' it’s all hands on deck
Skip to content
Subscribe today
Every print subscription comes with full digital access
Subscribe Now
By Carolyn Gramling
16 hours ago
Share this:
Share
Share via email (Opens in new window)
Email
Share on Facebook (Opens in new window)
Facebook
Share on Reddit (Opens in new window)
Reddit
Share on X (Opens in new window)
Print (Opens in new window)
Print
As documentaries about Earth’s accelerating climate crisis go, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is surprisingly buoyant.
The ocean covers more than two-thirds of Earth’s surface. And “as the climate heats up, our seas are under pressure like never before,” narrator Auli’i Cravalho, the voice of the title character in Disney’s Moana, says at the opening of The National Geographic Society’s new documentary. The film documents how oceanographers are racing to document and mitigate climate change’s impacts on ocean and coastal habitats.
Expedition: Saving Our Seas premieres November 13 on the National Geographic Channel at 9pm EST and streams the next day on Disney+ and Hulu.
Despite that solemn mission, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is full of hope — and stunning visuals. The documentary offers a window into the scientists’ wonder and joy in their work as they discover new life forms in the depths of the Southern Ocean, or successfully nurture young corals threatened by warming in the Pacific Ocean.
The film opens with a twist on the usual world map: At the center is one great ocean, surrounded by land. Trivia buffs know Earth has five oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. But geographic names aside, these five oceans are just one, linked by a global system of currents known as the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt.
“It’s this giant connected ocean that ignores all of the political boundaries, ignores all of the names we call them,” says Andrew Thurber, a biological oceanographer at the University of California, Santa Barbara, whose research is among those featured in the film.
The documentary loosely follows the current’s path as it zips around the world from project to project.
The first project in the documentary is Thurber’s. He’s on board a research vessel in the frigid Southern Ocean, which rings Antarctica. Using a remotely-operated vehicle dubbed SuBastian, Thurber and his colleagues are scanning the seafloor, hunting for the world’s southernmost hydrothermal vent.
Andrew Thurber, a National Geographic Explorer and associate professor of ecology, evolution and marine biology, analyzes data and images during one of ROV SuBastian’s explorations of the Antarctic benthos.
Luján Agusti/National Geographic
Hydrothermal vents spew superhot, chemically-enriched seawater. In the generally nutrient-poor Southern Ocean, that makes these vents a potential food oasis to support deep sea life.
Throughout the night, as the ROV scans the seafloor, Thurber and his colleagues stay glued to the video it sends back, oohing and aahing as never-before-seen life-forms come into view. “It was a marathon of excitement,” he says now.
Then they see it: A large black smoker, the southernmost hydrothermal vent ever found. And all around it: swarms of pregnant female krill.
“That blew all of our minds,” Thurber says. Krill are the keystone species of the entire Southern Ocean food web, a crucial food source for baleen whales, seals, penguins and fish. But krill are threatened by both industrial fishing and climate change. This discovery, Thurber says, helps make the case for a marine protected area, a region where fishing and other human activities should be restricted.
From the Southern Ocean, the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt flows thousands of kilometers to the north, where marine ecologist Maiyai Taal Hocheimy is tracking how the rising waters of the Atlantic Ocean are encroaching on Banjul, the capital of The Gambia in West Africa. Her hope is that salt-tolerant mangrove trees along the coast, with their dense network of soil-retaining roots, might help hold back the sea in the coming decades — provided that the community can be enlisted to help maintain the mangroves.
I found Hocheimy’s work especially inspiring because she is working to shape the future of oceanography. In 2017, she founded the GREAT (Gaining Research Experience in Africa for Tomorrow) Institute, the first aquatic and coastal science research institute in The Gambia. The mangrove project recruited young local scientists to help conduct the research.
“The goal is to train the next generation of environmental stewards,” Hocheimy says. “We have to show that mangroves have value, so they’ll understand and want to protect them. It is their future at stake.”
That sentiment is echoed many times in the film — the importance not only of enlisting young scientists but also centering local scientists who pose new questions that oceanographers who parachute in from other places may not think to ask, says marine biogeochemist Kristina Brown.
In the documentary, Brown, of the University of Manitoba in Canada, co-leads an expedition to explore the waters of Sherman Basin, a large bay north of the Arctic Circle in Nunavut, Canada. This region has been hunted and fished by Inuit people for centuries.
But it might change beyond all recognition in the next few decades, Brown says. So, the local Inuit community invited her to help create the first catalog of what species are present in the waters and on the seafloor. “[It’s] the first project I’ve been involved in where the local community both defined the research questions and have brought their own unique expertise to the research project.”
Watching how communities around the world are increasingly taking ownership of studies in their own waters was, for me, the most exciting takeaway of this documentary.

The brain’s fear center moonlights as the save button for memories

The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.
Neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience. Though the study doesn’t nail down the exact mechanism for memory formation, it points to a broader role for the amygdala within the memory-sorting apparatus.
The study probes an enduring quandary about the mind, says neuroscientist Jiayang Xiao of Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University in Los Angeles. “We forget much of what we experience … only a fraction of the information we encounter becomes a lasting memory,” she says.
Although a role for the amygdala in memory has been suggested before, previous studies that used electrodes reading brain activity through the scalp, or at the scale of thousands rather than individual neurons, captured a blurrier picture. It’s akin to a microphone recording from outside of a stadium, says cognitive neuroscientist Cory Inman at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who was not involved in the study.
“You might be able to tell that there’s a game happening. You might be able to tell when somebody scores a touchdown. You might even be able to tell that one side of the stadium is cheering for one team and another side of the stadium is cheering for another team,” but that’s about it, Inman says. The new study is more like a lapel mic pinned on a single fan in terms of scale and what the researchers were able to capture, adding clarity.
The amygdala, which is typically associated with regulating emotions like fear and aggression, has neurons that are challenging to reach, residing in two clusters deep within the brain. Xiao and her colleagues leveraged electrodes previously surgically implanted in more than 90 people with drug-resistant epilepsy to identify where seizures originate. In their new role, the electrodes singled out neurons involved in saving memories.
Patients were shown images of everyday objects belonging to five categories such as food and animals. About 10 to 30 minutes later, they attempted to recall which images were already shown. Xiao and her colleagues found that activity in certain amygdala neurons corresponded with an image being remembered. The image had been earmarked for longer term storage, Xiao says.
Although participants had to recall something from half an hour ago at most and the exact mechanism for saving memories is still unclear, the researchers think there are two main steps of the process. The team showed that individual neurons have a preference for one of the five categories of images. First the image is categorized by the amygdala. Then, the strength of the category neuron response the first time the image is shown dictates whether the image is later recalled.
A better understanding of this mechanism may pave the way for more effective treatments of memory disorders, Xiao says, a medical conundrum for which there are currently no broadly effective treatments.
The hippocampus is typically more directly linked to memory, so “it surprised me that we observe such a clear relationship between memory formation and activity in the amygdala,” Xiao says. By contrast, the correlation between hippocampus neuron activity and image recall was weaker and slightly delayed.
Future work like observing the impacts of stimulating amygdala neurons on memory will help researchers discern if this region can be targeted to improve memory, Xiao says.
For now, the secret to memory’s hidden machinations remains in the shadows.

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.
On November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos. The encounter marks the first time scientists will explore a pair of asteroids navigating the solar system together. To date, spacecraft have stopped to investigate just seven other asteroids, every one of them a lonely speck in outer space.
Hera will spend the coming weeks approaching Didymos and Dimorphos and will release two small companion spacecraft in January for an even closer look.
Didymos, a mass of rocks about twice as wide as the Empire State Building is tall, and its small moonlet Dimorphos have had a rough time lately. In 2022, NASA slammed its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft into Dimorphos, sending a plume of debris into space and shortening its orbit around Didymos by more than half an hour.
The cosmic realignment wasn’t a mere lark. Such an impact is one of the few ways scientists can practice planetary defense, the field dedicated to searching for dangerous asteroids and developing ways to deal with them lest humans go the way of the dinosaurs. DART and Hera are a carefully coordinated pair, with Hera’s top priority being to investigate the aftermath of DART’s crash and inform future planetary defense efforts.
That process will also yield a treasure trove of observations asteroid scientists are determined to exploit.
“Planetary defense and science are sort of two sides of the same coin,” says planetary scientist Jessica Sunshine of the University of Maryland, who was on the DART team but is not involved in the Hera mission. On the science side, she says, “we’re trying to figure out not so much how did we break the thing, but how was it put together in the first place.”
DART purposefully targeted a binary system instead of a solo asteroid to make measuring the change in orbit it accomplished easier: Any difference would be much more obvious against the 12-hour baseline orbit of Dimorphos around Didymos than against the months- or yearslong orbit of an asteroid circling the sun. (Despite the difficulty, scientists were able to calculate that DART shortened the more-than-two-year orbit of the Didymos system around the sun by a fraction of a second.)
Hera’s observations will provide a crucial glimpse at binary asteroids generally, which astronomers believe account for some 15 percent of all asteroids. Scientists expect that most binary asteroids in the inner solar system, including the Didymos system, probably formed their moonlets from debris that sloughed off the larger object then clumped together in orbit.
This image of Dimorphos was captured by the DART spacecraft in 2022 as it hurtled to an abrupt impact that shortened the moonlet’s orbit around Didymos by more than half an hour.
NASA/Johns Hopkins APL
Didymos spins so quickly that its gravity may not be strong enough to hold all its rock together. As the asteroid spins, it may send boulders into space, where they could end up landing on Dimorphos, continuing that material transfer today. Scientists will comb through Hera’s imagery for signs of rocks moving across each object’s surface, as well as between the two objects.
Scientists expect that Dimorphos is a rubble pile composed of boulders and rocky debris. It’s similar in structure to other recent spacecraft targets Ryugu and Bennu, although those are both significantly larger. The boulder-strewn landscape DART saw as it sped toward Dimorphos aligns with this theory, but how deep the rubbly structure extends is a mystery. “We’ve never seen the interior of an asteroid before,” says planetary scientist Angela Stickle of the Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory.
Juventas, Hera’s companion cubesat about the size of a breadbox, will change that. It carries a first-of-its-kind radar instrument to investigate Dimorphos’ internal structure.
Juventas will also attempt to land on Dimorphos, allowing scientists to directly interact with the surface. That’s a particularly tantalizing endeavor given one of the biggest surprises of NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission. When that spacecraft grabbed a sample of Bennu, it accidentally sank some half a meter into the rubble as the asteroid unexpectedly gave way beneath it, even though the surface had looked perfectly sturdy.
“Even though we had amazing images, the reaction was not what we expected,” says planetary scientist Patrick Michel of the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) of that experience. “There is still sort of a mismatch between what we see and what we feel.” He hopes that the Juventas landing will help scientists better connect appearance and reality on this front.
Although scientists will need to pick out the ways DART made Didymos and Dimorphos different from other binary asteroids, observations with Hera will offer new avenues for investigating more general questions in asteroid science.
For example, scientists know that before DART’s impact, Dimorphos always showed the same face to Didymos, just like our moon does to Earth. The collision probably changed that, sending Dimorphos tumbling — but there’s no way to know what state it’s in now because scientists have never seen this resetting process unfold. “Eventually, the system might stabilize, but we don’t know how long it takes,” says p

articles.title: Stone Age children left fingerprints on ancient art projects

Stone Age children left fingerprints on ancient art projects

Children have been making art with help from grown-ups for millennia.
Fragmented clay figurines dating as far back as 15,000 years ago, discovered in what is now Israel, preserve the fingerprints of both adults and young children. The finding suggests the grown-ups taught the kids how to shape and decorate clay, researchers report November 11 in PLOS One.
Children’s contributions to prehistoric art and culture aren’t well understood. Concrete evidence of their involvement has been hard to find, says archaeologist Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
In recent decades, researchers have found a handful of objects made by children — including 200,000-year-old rock art bearing child-sized handprints in Tibet and 30,000-year-old clay sculptures pockmarked with child-sized fingerprints in Czech Republic.
Davin and colleagues hadn’t set out to find Stone Age children’s artwork. They were investigating whether the Natufian culture — a group of hunter-gatherers who formed some of the first permanent settlements in the Levant about 14,000 years ago — made clay art before the advent of agriculture in the region.
The archaeologists came across the first set of fingerprints while sorting through 40 kilograms of clay collected at three Natufian sites, which range in age from 15,000 to 11,600 years old. Among tens of thousands of clay lumps, the team found some 150 fragments of sculptures, including 15 recognizable bird, gazelle and human figures. Around 60 of these pieces preserved fingerprints from where people had pinched or prodded the clay.
The distances between the fingerprints’ ridges, which are influenced by age and sex, suggest that most of the figurines were made by women and children — some younger than 10. Only a few sets of fingerprints belonged to men. And the torso of one tiny human statue had both adult and child fingerprints, hinting that an elder and child had passed it back and forth. Davin suspects that the adult actively taught a child how to work the clay.
The torso of this 14,500-year-old human figurine preserves the fingerprints of an adult (left) and child (right). Researchers think the adult taught the child how to shape the clay.
Laurent Davin (CC-BY 4.0)The torso of this 14,500-year-old human figurine preserves the fingerprints of an adult (left) and child (right). Researchers think the adult taught the child how to shape the clay.
Laurent Davin (CC-BY 4.0)
This evidence of intergenerational learning so far back in time is fascinating, says archaeologist Steven Dorland of Grand Valley State University in Allendale, Mich. It demonstrates how much researchers can learn from broadening their focus beyond adult males, he says. Dorland has used pottery to understand social learning in Indigenous societies of the Great Lakes region. He has even studied children’s fingerprints on some of those artifacts.
The purpose of the Natufian figurines is unclear. Most of the statues are less than 2 centimeters long and don’t display signs of intense use, the team found, suggesting they weren’t treated as precious heirlooms.
Davin suspects the figurines may have represented stories, like how kids draw Disney characters today, he says. “Maybe the idea is that the role of children here is not necessarily to learn to make figurines, but more to learn the story behind them.”

People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.
The fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology. Dubbed “dark magic mushrooms,” it is the first species of fungus discovered to make both types of compounds.
Chemist and fungal biologist Andrew Kunik found the dark magic mushroom in 2025 growing on a decaying moss-covered palm trunk in a central Florida wetland. Kunik, who was then doing post-baccalaureate research in the lab of fungal biologist Matthew Smith at the University of Florida in Gainesville, identified the mini mushroom as Galerina indica.
That species had not been reported in Florida before, Kunik says. “It’s quite rare and unusual.” He also found two other new related species, tagged with the placeholder names Galerina species 1 and Galerina species 2.
Other researchers had previously described G. indica’s appearance and found DNA signatures that distinguish the fungus from related species. But no one had cataloged the mushroom’s complete chemical or genetic makeup.
Related Galerina species make amatoxins, deadly chemicals that can kill in even tiny amounts and are found in death cap mushrooms and other species. Kunik and colleagues looked for those toxins in G. indica and the two other new Galerina species. G. indica makes a previously undiscovered form of amatoxin the team is calling alpha-proamanitin, the chemical analysis revealed.
The small mushroom also had blue bruises, a clue that it might make psilocybin, a psychedelic chemical being tested as a treatment for mental health disorders. Fungi usually make either amatoxin or psilocybin. Not both. Galerina species 1 also makes psilocybin but doesn’t make amatoxin, and species 2 makes neither.
“This finding shows that there’s a lot more diversity in [fungal] chemistry and the ways that they’re combined than we had really thought about,” says Anne Pringle, a mycologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the work.
Dark magic mushrooms are tiny. A cluster of full-grown Galerina indica mushroom caps (right) can fit on Andrew Kunik’s thumbnail (left).
Andrew R. Kunik
Discovering these dual compounds in one mushroom was both exciting and required further analysis to confirm, Kunik says. “Surprising discoveries require great depth of evidence,” he says.
A complete workup of the mushroom’s DNA revealed genes for producing both types of chemicals. Ancestors of these dark magic mushrooms probably picked up those genes by swapping DNA with other species. Such DNA swapping, called horizontal gene transfer, is one way that organisms can quickly evolve new traits, like when bacteria exchange antibiotic resistance genes with unrelated species.
Ancestors of G. indica and its relatives probably acquired amatoxin genes early on. Those toxins are made by many of G. indica’s cousins, which indicates that amatoxins are probably heirlooms passed down from common ancestors. Ancestors of species 1 and species 2 seem to have dropped the amatoxin genes at some point since they no longer make the compounds.
The two psilocybin-producing species may have independently obtained the psychedelic genes in separate DNA swap meets, or a common ancestor may have picked up the genes and then passed them down to G. indica and species 1. There’s not enough known about the fungi’s family tree to sort out which scenario is correct.
And there’s another unsolved evolutionary mystery, Pringle says. “We still don’t know why mushrooms are poisonous.” Many scientists think it is for defending against predators, but hard evidence is lacking, she says.
“Can I eat it?” is often the first question people ask when finding a new mushroom, Pringle says. “I’m always so uncomfortable with that question and that conversation. And this paper confirms that, in fact, you should be uncomfortable.” After all, eating these dark magic mushrooms could send people tripping into the grave.

Physicist Stefano Martiniani has designed an entirely new class of materials that blurs the line between order and chaos. Called gyromorphs, these metamaterials rely on crystal-like geometric structure and liquidlike randomness to block light from penetrating at any angle.
Physicists thought, structurally speaking, that they could not create such hybrid materials. “But this is evidence that you can, under certain constraints,” says Martiniani, of New York University. He likens the gyromorphs’ disorderliness to a crowd of people. You could see through the crowd if individuals stood still in straight lines, but not if they are clustered together in random groups. But there’s order too: From anywhere you stand in a gyromorph crowd, you’ll see a ring of people at a given distance.
Gyromorphs are a type of metamaterial, a substance with a structure designed to give it properties not found in naturally occurring materials. Metamaterials can control light, sound or other waves, and are often used in smartphones, medical imaging and computers. Martiniani says gyromorphs could be used to make more energy-efficient optical computers, which use light to process and store data.
To design a gyromorph, Martiniani needed to find a way to achieve the perfect structural balance. He turned to FReSCo, a program his lab created that designs molecular structures to meet researchers’ specifications, for help. “We had an algorithm, we gave it an objective, and then it was able to solve that objective, finding a solution that we were not expecting,” he says. “That is the best kind of discovery.”

Cartwheeling seems like it should require both arms and legs. But some itty-bitty snakes in Southeast Asia manage it without either.
Scientists first shared snapshots of a dwarf reed snake (Pseudorabdion longiceps) cartwheeling away from danger in 2023. Now, videos of three Pseudorabdion species hightailing it down a racetrack in the lab have offered a closer look at this rare and strangely acrobatic behavior.
Each snake starts with its body curled into a C shape, head lifted off the ground and facing the way it’s going. It then whips its tail out behind it, briefly becoming airborne. The snake flips its tail forward and down past its head. When the snake’s tail hits the ground in front of it, another roll begins, researchers report October 19 in Current Biology.
“What a cool snake behavior,” says Jessica Tingle, a biologist at Brown University in Providence, R.I., not involved in the work. “I find it especially amazing that an elongate animal like a snake can manage to roll, especially given that they do it in such an explosive way, which probably asks a lot of their muscles and bones.”
Watch a Pseudorabdion saravacense cartwheel down a racetrack in the lab. Videos like this helped researchers pinpoint how these snakes perform their gymnastics.
Y. Kojima et al/Current Biology 2026
Yosuke Kojima was equally surprised when a colleague in Sarawak, Malaysia recounted witnessing this “very weird” behavior in 2019. So the researchers collected snakes from Malaysia’s Kubah National Park. They scooped up 11 P. saravacense, one P. collaris, one P. longiceps, plus six Calamaria reed snakes for comparison.
Finding the snakes was no easy task. They were only about 11 to 28 centimeters long. “They always hide under the leaves,” says Kojima, an ecologist at Toho University in Chiba, Japan. But were any of the snakes able to cartwheel away from the researchers? “No,” Kojima laughs. “We are quicker than them.”
The team set up a 2.2-meter-long racetrack and placed the snakes one at a time at one end. A gentle tap coaxed the snakes to move and cameras above and beside the track recorded the action. None of the Calamaria snakes cartwheeled, but all of the Pseudorabdion snakes did. At full tilt, they tumbled at 1.7 to 3.7 meters per second — about six to 13 kilometers per hour.
Through it all, the snakes held their heads fairly steady — reminiscent of how flying snakes hold their heads stable while launching into the air, the researchers say.
Round and round
A cartwheeling snake first rolls its body along the ground to whip its tail out behind its head. Then, it swings its tail up and over its head. Finally, it brings its tail down on either the left or right side of its head. Once it the tail hits the ground, the snake is ready for another roll. In the cartwheel seen on top, the snake brings its tail down on the left side of its head, angling its whitish belly toward the viewer. In the cartwheel on the bottom, the snake’s tail lands on the right side of its head, showing its darker back to the viewer.
Yosuke Kojima, Kanon Tanaka
“I am very curious how such a strange and possibly demanding movement evolved … whether dwarf reed snakes have something special in their anatomy, physiology or neural control that lets them do it when their close relatives apparently can’t or don’t,” Tingle says. “Are their brains different in some way to let them coordinate a fast and unusual movement? Or do all snakes have the basic equipment, and they just don’t use it?”
Those may be open mysteries. But catching snakes cartwheeling on camera does tie up one loose end for Tingle.
“Some writers in the 1800s talked about ‘hoop snakes’ and described their motion as rolling, but that seemed pretty fantastical to me, and I chalked it up to overly inventive imaginations,” Tingle says. Those 19th century authors may or may not have been describing the exact behavior Kojima’s team recorded. “Either way, it’s neat to find out a real animal does something reminiscent of a fantastical old story.”

articles.title: Going the distance
articles.text:
Voyager 1 is now one light-day from Earth. What’s out there?
Skip to content

By Lisa Grossman

NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft has been breaking distance records for decades. Launched almost 50 years ago, it became the farthest human-built object from Earth when it overtook the pathfinding Pioneer 10 probe in 1998. It was the first spacecraft to leave the solar system’s protective bubble, and it will be humankind’s first emissary to the stars.
The cameras on Voyager 1, along with those on its twin spacecraft, Voyager 2, captured powerful megastorms in the outer solar system, the first images of dozens of moons and never-before-seen details of the gossamer rings around Jupiter, Saturn, Neptune and Uranus. The images and data sent home have shaped theories of how the solar system formed and evolved, inspired subsequent missions and posed enough new questions to keep space scientists busy for decades.
And this month, Voyager 1 will set another big record. On November 18 at 5:16:07 a.m. Eastern Standard Time, it will become the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth: the distance light travels in 24 hours. That’s a journey of 25.9 billion kilometers, or more than four times the distance from the sun to Pluto. At that point, signals from Earth will take a full day to reach Voyager 1; it will take another day to hear back.
“I just never imagined [the mission] would last that long,” says Linda Spilker, a planetary scientist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif., who began working on Voyager shortly before the probes launched in 1977. Spilker was in Cape Canaveral, Fla., for the first launch. She even planned the births of her children, now in their 40s, around mission milestones. After stepping away to lead another mission, she is now back as Voyager head scientist.
Two other scientists have been with Voyager since the beginning. Others weren’t yet born when the spacecraft launched. “Voyager, to this day, is a multi-generational mission,” Spilker says. But it isn’t a mission of nostalgia. There’s still a world of discovery out beyond the solar system’s edge.
“Every piece of data, every day that goes by that we get data from the Voyagers, tells us something new,” says physicist Jamie Rankin of Princeton University, who started her Ph.D. in August 2012, the same month that Voyager 1 left the solar system for the cold, calm seas of interstellar space. “Every day, it’s in places nobody’s ever explored before.”
Exploring our neighborhood
The original mission of the Voyager probes was to explore the outer parts of our solar system, which until then had remained largely mysterious. A rare planetary alignment meant that a spacecraft launched in the late 1970s could swoop past Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, getting a gravitational boost from each planet that it passed. With these gravitational assists, the spacecraft could complete the tour in less than 15 years. Such an alignment won’t happen again until the 2150s.
Whorls and vortices in Jupiter’s atmosphere captured by Voyager 1 in March 1979. JPL-Caltech/NASA
Neptune’s perpetual storm, the Great Dark Spot, seen by Voyager 2 in August 1989. JPL-Caltech/NASA
The heavily cratered surface of Jupiter’s moon Callisto as seen by Voyager 1 in March 1979. JPL-Caltech/NASA
Uranus as seen by Voyager 2 in January 1986. JPL-Caltech/NASA
Saturn and its rings captured in November 1980, four days after Voyager 1’s closest approach to the planet. JPL-Caltech/NASA
An active plume (blue) on Jupiter’s moon Io is visible in this mosaic of images from Voyager 1. JPL-Caltech/NASA, USGS
The project was a bold step for its time. When work began in the early 1970s, no spacecraft had gone farther than Mars. NASA set a conservative goal for the mission: flybys of Jupiter and Saturn. In 1972 and 1973, NASA launched two Pioneer probes, which made sure the trek was possible and gathered data along the way. As with Voyager, there were two spacecraft in case one failed.
After nail-biting launches and a wait of nearly two years, the Voyagers began uncovering many of Jupiter’s and Saturn’s long-held secrets, including the volcanoes on Jupiter’s moon Io, details of Jupiter’s Great Red Spot and hints of geologic activity on Saturn’s moon Enceladus.
Mission accomplished, Voyager 2 went on to pass Uranus and Neptune. It took the first images of the planets’ rings and discovered more than a dozen moons along the way. The spacecraft also spotted a perpetually churning storm on Neptune and erupting geysers on Neptune’s moon Triton.
“The highlights of Voyager were clearly the planetary encounters,” said Ed Stone, the mission’s original head scientist, in a NASA interview before his death in 2024. “We had a lifetime of discovery packed into each one.”
Linda Morabito (left image, at center) and Linda Spilker (right image, front right) are shown with other mission personnel. JPL-Caltech/NASA; NASA
The uncontested stars of these encounters were the images shared in news reports and TV broadcasts as the planets and their moons came into view. Jupiter’s moon Io turned out to be a shocking splotchy orange color that looked like a pizza.
A humble navigation image of that moon led to one of the most surprising discoveries of the entire mission. Four days past Voyager 1’s closest approach to Jupiter, after the excitement had died down, project astronomer Linda Morabito of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory started processing additional images of Io. These images had been taken after the flyby, when Voyager was looking back over its shoulder.
As
